metadata.title: GM is pitching itself more as a tech company like Tesla

content.text:
If you can't beat tech companies, join them. General Motors (GM) said Tuesday it will move its stock listing from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq, home of many of Silicon Valley's biggest names, in an effort to repitch the legacy Detroit automaker as a tech-forward enterprise.
Even sitting close to names like Apple (AAPL) and Amazon (AMZN) can have a spillover effect, as investors cling to the excitement around AI and tech's overall influence in steering the market. Labels matter — remember Domino's (DPZ) identity as "a technology company that happens to sell pizza?"
Walmart (WMT), another name you might not associate with cutting-edge tech, made the same change to the Nasdaq earlier this year as it embraces its own AI and advertising transformation.
"GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," said Paul Jacobson, the company's CFO, in a statement on Tuesday.
The undisputed heavyweight champion of this move is Elon Musk. Tesla (TSLA) hasn't been a "car company" for years — certainly if you look at its valuation — and SpaceX (SPCX) is no longer a rocket company. (Still, GM has done well.)
And investors have bought these arguments. Both companies have valuations commensurate with being an AI/robotics/robotaxi giant or an AI/datacenter/chipmaker giant. A much-talked-about merger with SpaceX would put an even finer point on what Tesla is.
Of course, GM does not have these activities to make its case.
But in some respects the shift makes sense. Newer vehicles have enhanced safety and steering features that make driving meaningfully different than sitting behind the wheel of the car you got your license in. GM, like other automakers, is outfitting its vehicles with more sophisticated software and sensors. The company announced last week it's working to reduce its development cycle by half through AI tools and virtualization.
Some observers are skeptical of the new sales pitch, however.
"Cars are the first robots out there in the wild," Envorso founder Adrian Balfour said on Yahoo Finance's Morning Hang on Tuesday. "If it was a data play or if it was a robotics play, I could really see it. But without that, I'm not sure."
Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban.
